explain.say: Plastics are not all the same. A drinks bottle, a yoghurt pot and a carrier bag are different chemicals that do not mix well when melted, so recycling starts with collecting and sorting them.

explain.say: The pellets go back to factories to be moulded or spun into new things, like bottles, fleece jackets and pipes. Each melt shortens the plastic's long molecules, so most plastic can only be recycled a few times.

faq.a: Near-infrared sensors shine light on each item and read the reflected pattern, which is like a fingerprint for each type of plastic. A computer then fires a precise puff of air to knock the item into the right chute.
asks: How does a recycling plant know what plastic it is?

faq.q: What do the numbers on plastic mean?
faq.a: The number inside the triangle is a resin code naming the plastic type: 1 is PET, used for drinks bottles; 2 is HDPE, for milk bottles; 5 is polypropylene, for tubs. It does not promise the item is recycled where you live.
asks: What does the recycling triangle number mean?

faq.q: Why can't all plastic be recycled?
faq.a: Some items mix several plastics or materials that cannot be separated, films and bags jam machines, food contamination ruins batches, and black plastic often cannot be seen by the infrared sorters.
asks: Why is black plastic hard to recycle?

faq.q: How many times can plastic be recycled?
faq.a: Usually only a few times. Heating and melting breaks some of the long polymer chains, so the plastic becomes weaker each time, and new plastic is often mixed in.
Recycled PET can become new bottles, food trays or polyester fibre for fleece and carpets; HDPE can become pipes, bins and garden furniture.
asks: What is made from recycled plastic bottles?

facts: Black plastic is hard to sort because the carbon black pigment absorbs the near-infrared light that sorting sensors use.
A 2017 study by Roland Geyer and colleagues estimated that only about 9 percent of all plastic ever made had been recycled.
